# Optical telegraph (semaphore network) (`optical_telegraph`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/communication.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Communication & information (`communication`)
- Deps: helped by telescope, signal_beacons_flag_codes
- Core idea: A chain of towers on high points 10–15 km apart, each with a mechanism of movable arms (Chappe: a crossbar with two arms set by ropes and pulleys) or shutters (Murray, Edelcrantz). An operator reads the next tower through a telescope and repeats each sign. A codebook turns pairs of signs into numbered words and phrases, so few signs make a sentence. On the Paris–Lille line a single sign could travel some 200 km in minutes. A dispatch took longer: the operators had to relay a succession of signs, and poor visibility could interrupt transmission. Add rules for repeating back and correcting errors.
- Pitfalls:
  - Placing towers too far apart or hidden by haze: reliable distance is about 10–15 km even with telescopes
  - Sending letter by letter instead of with a phrase codebook
  - Forgetting that night, fog and rain stop the line
  - Assuming privacy: operators and watchers can read the signs, so use codes; France made it a state monopoly (1837)
- History: europe: 1684 – Robert Hooke proposes a signalling system to the Royal Society; 1792 Chappe's demonstration; 1794 Paris–Lille line reports the recapture of Condé; 1794–1796 Edelcrantz in Sweden and Murray's shutter line London–Deal; 1832 Prussian line Berlin–Koblenz; by the 1840s France has over 500 stations; replaced by the electric telegraph from the 1850s
- Read:
  - Gerard J. Holzmann & Björn Pehrson, The Early History of Data Networks (1995)
  - Ignace Chappe, Histoire de la télégraphie (1824)
